meta.title: NORRAID AFRICA – Humanity Without Borders
meta.description: NORRAID AFRICA is a Sweden-based humanitarian association standing with families facing emergencies in Sudan, DR Congo and South Sudan.

common.fallback_note: This text is shown in English until a translation is approved.

sudan.name: Sudan
sudan.lead: Well into its third year, the conflict in Sudan continues to drive a humanitarian and protection crisis of catastrophic scale.
intro: Civilians have been forced from their homes again and again. Hospitals, schools and markets have been attacked, and landmines and unexploded ordnance litter large parts of the country.

According to the UN's 2026 humanitarian plan, every locality in Sudan is assessed at severity level 3 or above, and in Darfur and Kordofan more than 80 per cent of the local population need humanitarian assistance.
sudan.food: Mass hunger has taken hold in large parts of the country. The UN reports 29 million people acutely food insecure and 23 areas in or at risk of famine. Three quarters of female-headed households are estimated to be food insecure.
sudan.water: More than half of people across Sudan report difficulties in accessing safe water, while water and sanitation systems are crumbling under the strain of conflict.
sudan.health: Fewer than 30 per cent of health facilities are functioning in the worst-affected areas. Cholera, malaria and dengue are spreading as the health system collapses.
sudan.displacement: As of October 2025, 9.6 million people remained internally displaced inside Sudan, many in extremely precarious conditions. About 2.6 million people have returned since November 2024, mainly to Khartoum and Aj Jazirah.
sudan.education: Schools have been attacked or turned into shelters for displaced families. Children face recruitment, abduction and other grave violations, and need protection and safe places to learn.
sudan.regions: Regions highlighted: Darfur and Kordofan states, Khartoum and Aj Jazirah, which the 2026 plan names among the areas of most severe need or priority response.
priorities: Support for primary health care and cholera prevention
Protection and psychosocial support for women and children

drc.name: DR Congo
drc.tag: One of the largest displacement crises in the world
drc.lead: Armed conflict remains the main driver of humanitarian needs in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, especially in North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri.
intro: In 2025, hostilities expanded across the eastern provinces, causing massive new displacement, repeated movement back and forth, and serious protection risks for civilians.
Despite the country's vast natural resources, poverty and vulnerability remain among the highest in the world. Epidemics and climate-related floods and landslides add to the pressure on families.
drc.food: Food insecurity has reached extreme levels: the UN projects 26.6 million people in crisis or emergency food insecurity (IPC phases 3 and 4) between January and June 2026.
drc.water: Communities affected by the crisis name safe water, hygiene and sanitation among their main priorities, alongside nutritious food and primary health care.
drc.health: Cholera, measles and mpox continue to pose significant risks, especially where response capacity is limited. Recent Ebola outbreaks were contained, but the risk of resurgence persists.
drc.displacement: More than 5.3 million people were internally displaced as of September 2025, and more than 3 million returns were recorded during 2025, including unplanned returns after site closures.
drc.education: Children, women and girls, persons with disabilities and survivors of gender-based violence face disproportionate risks. Families displaced again and again struggle to keep children in school.
drc.regions: Regions highlighted: North Kivu and South Kivu. Ituri, also named among the most acute areas, is part of the former Orientale province on this simplified map.
priorities: Food and nutrition support for displaced families
Clean water and sanitation in displacement sites
Health support including cholera and measles prevention

south-sudan.name: South Sudan
south-sudan.tag: Two thirds of the population need help
south-sudan.lead: South Sudan is facing a convergence of humanitarian, economic, security, health and climate crises, made worse by people fleeing the war in Sudan.
intro: About two thirds of the country's population need humanitarian assistance in 2026. Families are caught in cycles of violence, floods and disease outbreaks.
Since 2019, annual flooding has affected more than one million people each year. As of November 2025, about 1.3 million people had arrived from Sudan.
south-sudan.food: More than 7.5 million people are projected to face crisis or worse levels of hunger (IPC 3+) during the April–July 2026 lean season. Some 2.1 million children aged 6–59 months are expected to suffer acute malnutrition.
south-sudan.water: Repeated floods damage water points and latrines, and the country is facing the worst cholera outbreak in its history, with more than 95,000 cases recorded since September 2024.
south-sudan.health: Around 1.1 million pregnant and breastfeeding women are at risk of malnutrition and in need of treatment. Funding shortfalls and attacks on aid workers are forcing health services to close.
south-sudan.displacement: An estimated 2.6 million people remain internally displaced, many for more than a decade. In 2025 alone, more than 675,000 people were newly displaced by conflict and floods.
south-sudan.education: Conflict, floods and displacement keep many children out of school. Communities often organise learning under trees or in temporary shelters.
south-sudan.regions: Regions highlighted: Upper Nile, Unity and Jonglei, where the 2026 plan reports the greatest needs and the most severe access constraints.
priorities: Nutrition support for children and mothers
Emergency relief for families displaced by floods

mission.title: Our Mission
mission.lead: To stand with families facing humanitarian emergencies in Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and South Sudan — with honesty, dignity and full transparency.
why: Sudan, DR Congo and South Sudan together account for more than 60 million people in need of humanitarian assistance in 2026, according to UN-coordinated plans. At the same time, funding has fallen sharply and aid agencies have been forced to cut life-saving programmes.
NORRAID AFRICA was founded as an association in Sweden to connect people in Europe with families in these three countries, through an accountable and transparent organisation.
mission.countries: The three crises are connected. People fleeing the war in Sudan cross into South Sudan, while eastern DR Congo faces one of the largest displacement crises in the world. All three are among the most severe and the most underfunded emergencies.

values.d: We show people as they are: resilient, never helpless. We protect privacy, especially of children.
We never invent stories, statistics or urgency.
We publish who receives donations, how funds are used and our sources.
We are nonpartisan and help people based on need alone.
We work through local organisations that know their communities best.

mission.partners_title: How we intend to work with local partners
partners: We work with established local and national organisations in Sudan, DR Congo and South Sudan.
Before any transfer, partners are checked: registration, track record, financial controls and safeguarding policies.
Every partnership is governed by a written agreement with a budget, reporting requirements and the right to audit.
Every programme is monitored on the ground, from distribution to follow-up with the families we serve.
gov: NORRAID AFRICA is an association based in Sweden, run by a board accountable to its members.
Roles are separated: content editors cannot approve finances, and finance reviewers verify every reported expense.
Annual accounts and project reports are prepared every year.

about.title: About Us
about.lead: NORRAID AFRICA — Humanity Without Borders — is a humanitarian association based in Sweden.
body: We are an association in Sweden dedicated to helping families affected by conflict, hunger and displacement in Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and South Sudan.

Together with our donors and local partners we have supported more than 22,000 families and completed hundreds of humanitarian projects: food, medical care, clean water, shelter and help for children.
We believe trust is earned through transparency: clear about who receives donations, how they are used and where every figure comes from.

samira-kassala.title: Samira's escape from Khartoum
samira-kassala.summary: Samira, 22, fled fighting in Khartoum in 2023 and now lives in a school turned into a shelter in Kassala.
body: Samira was 20 when fighting reached Khartoum in 2023. Like millions of Sudanese, she fled. Today she lives in the Omar Haj Musa School in Kassala, a school building repurposed to shelter displaced families.

Remembering the journey, she describes holding her breath at every checkpoint, afraid of being stopped and taken. Her account, recorded by the UN, reflects the protection risks women and girls face throughout Sudan's war.
samira-kassala.context: Kassala in eastern Sudan hosts large numbers of people displaced from Khartoum and other conflict areas, many in schools and public buildings.
samira-kassala.needs: Safe shelter, protection from violence, psychosocial support and a way to rebuild her life.
chronology: April 2023: war breaks out in Khartoum
2023: Samira flees through checkpoints to Kassala
December 2025: her story is published by UN OCHA

tumaini-sake.title: Tumaini returns to a home that is gone
tumaini-sake.summary: Tumaini, 39, came back with her family to Sake in North Kivu after fleeing. Their house was destroyed; they now live under a tarpaulin on the same plot.
body: When conflict reached Sake, in North Kivu, Tumaini and her family fled. After the closure of displacement sites around Goma, they returned to their compound — only to find their home destroyed.

Today the family lives under a tarpaulin on the spot where their house once stood. Their story, reported by the UN, is shared by many of the more than 3 million people recorded as returning in eastern DR Congo in 2025.
tumaini-sake.context: In 2025, hostilities expanded across North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri. Many families returned after site closures, often to destroyed homes and without services.
tumaini-sake.needs: Shelter materials, household items, food and access to clean water and health care.
chronology: 2025: Tumaini's family flees fighting near Sake
2025: displacement sites around Goma close; the family returns
December 2025: her story is published by UN OCHA

qisma-bor.title: Five years in a camp in Bor
qisma-bor.summary: For five years, Qisma, her husband and their five children have lived in Bor Town's former displacement camp in South Sudan.
body: Qisma and her family have spent five years in the former displacement camp in Bor Town, Jonglei State. Their life has been shaped by displacement, floods and the struggle to provide for five children.
Her story, published by the UN with the 2026 South Sudan humanitarian plan, is one of millions behind the figure of 2.6 million people still internally displaced in South Sudan.
qisma-bor.context: Jonglei is among the states most affected by floods and conflict. Many displaced families have lived in camps for years.
qisma-bor.needs: Food, nutrition support for the children, clean water, health care and a durable solution for the family.
chronology: Around 2021: the family settles in the camp in Bor Town
2025: renewed conflict and floods displace hundreds of thousands more
January 2026: her story is published by UN OCHA

lala-ali-jamam.title: Eight days on foot to reach safety
lala-ali-jamam.summary: Lala Ali, 20, walked for eight days with her child to escape fighting in Sudan's Blue Nile State and reach Jamam refugee camp in South Sudan.
body: In early 2012, fighting was coming closer to Lala Ali's home in Sudan's Blue Nile State. She decided to leave. With her child, she walked for eight days to the border, carrying water, but without enough food.

She arrived at the Jamam refugee camp in South Sudan in February 2012, one of tens of thousands of people who fled Blue Nile that year. Her words were recorded by the UK Department for International Development.
lala-ali-jamam.context: This story dates from 2012. It shows how long people have been fleeing between Sudan and South Sudan — a movement that continues today, with about 1.3 million arrivals from Sudan since 2023.
lala-ali-jamam.needs: In 2012: food, safe water, shelter and health care in the camp.
chronology: Early 2012: fighting spreads in Blue Nile State
February 2012: Lala arrives in Jamam camp after eight days on foot
April 2012: photographed and interviewed by DFID

nyadil-lankien.title: Counting the days until the grain runs out
nyadil-lankien.summary: In 2015, Nyadil Machar, a farmer in Lankien, Jonglei, explained that her millet would last until May. After that, her family would have to eat leaves.
body: Nyadil Machar grows millet near Lankien, in northern Jonglei. In March 2015 she told Oxfam that her harvest would last until May. After that, she said, the family would have to eat leaves — there was no other option.
Before the crisis, families could move elsewhere when their grain ran out. Conflict had closed most supply routes and made that impossible.
nyadil-lankien.context: This story dates from 2015. Hunger in South Sudan remains severe: more than 7.5 million people are projected to face crisis-level hunger in the 2026 lean season.
nyadil-lankien.needs: Food assistance during the lean season, seeds and tools, and safe access to markets.
chronology: 2013: conflict breaks out in South Sudan
March 2015: Nyadil speaks with Oxfam in Lankien
Lean season (May onwards): food stocks run out

sources.title: Sources and Methodology
sources.lead: How we choose, check and present humanitarian statistics.
rules: We use figures published by UN agencies and humanitarian coordination bodies, mainly UN OCHA's Global Humanitarian Overview and country Humanitarian Needs and Response Plans.
Every statistic records its value, unit, country, definition, reporting year, source organisation, source link and the date we last verified it.
We keep three categories strictly apart: people in need, people targeted for assistance, and people actually reached.
When a plan is revised, we show the current figure and explain the change. Outdated figures are withdrawn, not left online.
We never round up, combine incompatible figures or present sector-wide results as our own.
Photographs come from licensed sources such as Wikimedia Commons. Each image shows the photographer, licence and source.

sections.p: NORRAID AFRICA, a humanitarian association based in Sweden, is responsible for personal data processed on this website. Contact us through the contact page.

Newsletter: your email address, language and the date and time of your consent. Contact form: your name, email and message. Donations: we record the fund and amount you selected before leaving for PayPal, without any personal data. We do not collect card or bank details.

sections.h: Why and on what legal basis
sections.p: Newsletter emails are sent with your consent (GDPR article 6.1.a), which you can withdraw at any time. Contact messages are processed to answer you (legitimate interest, article 6.1.f). Accounting records are kept to meet legal obligations (article 6.1.c).
When you donate, PayPal (Europe) S.à r.l. et Cie, S.C.A. processes your payment as an independent controller under its own privacy statement.
Newsletter data is kept until you unsubscribe. Contact messages are deleted after 24 months. Accounting records are kept for the period required by Swedish law.
We do not sell or rent personal data and never import purchased or scraped email lists. Data is stored with our web hosting provider in the EU/EEA.
You have the right to access, correct, delete, restrict or port your data and to object to processing. You can complain to the Swedish Authority for Privacy Protection (IMY).
nr_lang remembers the language you chose (1 year). nr_ft protects our forms against misuse (session). Both are strictly necessary or functional first-party cookies and do not track you.
We do not use advertising or tracking cookies. If privacy-friendly analytics are ever enabled, they will only run after you agree.

Some images may load directly from Wikimedia Commons until a local copy is stored. Wikimedia may receive your IP address under its own privacy policy. PayPal sets its own cookies only when you visit paypal.com.
This website is operated by NORRAID AFRICA, a humanitarian association based in Sweden.
We take care to publish accurate, sourced information. Humanitarian figures change; each statistic shows its source and the date we last verified it.
Photographs are used under the licences shown with each image. Our own texts and logo may not be reused without permission.
We are not liable for the content of external websites we link to.
These terms are governed by Swedish law.
Donations are currently received through a personal PayPal account registered in Sweden. It is not the account of a registered charity. The account holder is shown on the donation page and on PayPal.
Donations to NORRAID AFRICA are not tax-deductible.
Each donation is recorded against the fund the donor selects (Sudan, DR Congo, South Sudan or general) and used for our programmes there.
Donations are confirmed only from PayPal records. We never publish donation totals that have not been confirmed, and we never show invented donor activity, matching offers or countdowns.
Contact us within 30 days with your PayPal transaction ID. We will help you request a refund through PayPal.

sections.h: If a programme cannot go ahead
sections.p: If funds cannot be used in the chosen country, they will be used for our general humanitarian fund in the other focus countries.
We aim to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA.

Semantic HTML, keyboard navigation with visible focus, text alternatives for images, sufficient colour contrast, support for reduced motion, right-to-left layout for Arabic, and forms with clear labels and error messages.
Some country maps are simplified illustrations; the same information is always given in text. Older photographs may have limited descriptions from their original sources.
If you find a barrier, please tell us through the contact page. We aim to respond within 14 days.
